function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I don’t have the ability to run `git` commands or write files directly into your local filesystem from here, but I can walk you through exactly what you’d do locally (or in a CI script) and give you ready‑to‑copy templates for each of the artifacts you asked for.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re doing this inside a CI job, make sure the runner has SSH keys set up so it can pull from the private repo.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick scan to see what the entry point is, what dependencies exist, etc.:

```bash
cat package.json
```

Typical output might look like:

```json
{
  "name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "app.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node app.js"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.18.2"
  }
}
```

From this we know:

* The app starts with `npm start` → `node app.js`
* It listens on port `3000` (check `app.js` for `app.listen(3000)`)

### 2.2 Create/Update Dockerfile

Create a minimal Dockerfile that installs deps and runs the app:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Default command
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

If a Dockerfile already exists, replace its contents with the snippet above (or merge intelligently).

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a `k8s/deployment.yaml` (and optionally a `service.yaml`) under a new folder called `k8s`:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # adjust tag as needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you prefer
```

> **Note** – Replace `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with whatever registry/tag you’ll push to.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Add a `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up QEMU
      uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: ~/.cache/docker
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-docker-${{ hashFiles('Dockerfile') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-docker-

    - name: Build and push
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

Make sure you store your Docker Hub credentials (`DOCKERHUB_USERNAME`, `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`) as *repository secrets* in GitHub.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you added a `k8s/service.yaml`, include that too.

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, building the image and pushing it to Docker Hub.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile (in repo root) |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` (and optional `service.yaml`) |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` |
| ✅ | Secrets set in GitHub repo settings |
| ✅ | Commit & push |

That’s everything you need to get the repo containerised, deployed to Kubernetes, and continuously built via GitHub Actions. Let me know if you’d like help automating any part of this process (e.g., writing a small script that does all the `git` commands for you).
